paper_title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Video diffusion models (Ho et al., 2022b,a; Singer et al., 2023; Blattmann et al., 2023) synthesize realistic videos (Wang et al., 2025; Seedance Team et al., 2026; Black Forest Labs, 2026; MiniMax, 2026), compose diverse scenes and visual concepts (Deng et al., 2026; Chou et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026), and respond to camera and action controls (Wang et al., 2024; He et al., 2025). In particular, autoregressive (AR) models (Jin et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Teng et al., 2025) generate videos incrementally, allowing them to incorporate new controls or observations. They are promising medium for interactive visual applications, such as world simulation (Chou et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026), games (Yu et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026), and predictive models for robotics (Ye et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026). Recent works have significantly accelerated AR video diffusion models, primarily through distillation and fewstep sampling (Yin et al., 2024a, 2025). Some now report real-time generation speeds based on frames per second (FPS) (Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026). However, FPS alone does not establish whether model can respond to user inputs in real time. For instance, model that generates 30-frame clip as single batch in one second achieves 30 FPS, but the user must still wait one second to see response. Seamless real-time interactivity demands low input-to-response latency, as established in interactive systems research (Miller, 1968). Human-computer interaction studies have reported delay-detection thresholds of approximately 50 to 60 ms (Annett et al., 2014; Deber et al., 2015; Forch et al., 2017). 1 Thus, we target end-to-end per-frame latency below 50 ms. We define this latency as the delay between the arrival of new input signal (e.g., steering command) and the presentation of the first RGB frame that depicts its effects. In the baseline methods we study (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a), the inference pipeline consists of KV cache updates, diffusion sampling, and pixel rendering. Measuring latency requires accounting for the complete critical path through these operations. We also report the corresponding responses per second (RPS), defined as RPS = 1/Ls = 1,000/Lms, where Ls and Lms denote this latency in seconds and milliseconds, respectively. Each generation unit counts as one response, regardless of how many frames it produces. Unlike FPS, which amortizes generation time over the frames in batch, RPS directly measures responsiveness for interactive applications; an interactive latency target of 50 ms corresponds to 20 RPS. As shown in Fig. 1, the fastest baselines remain well below the target response rate. Figure 1 Quality-speed tradeoff. VBench scores vs. per-frame latency. Upper left is better. Only FastFrames meets an acceptable threshold (Deber et al., 2015) for seamless interactivity ( 50 ms latency, equivalently 20 responses per second (RPS)) while matching or exceeding comparable baselines in visual quality. To close this gap, we introduce FastFrames, family of autoregressive video diffusion models that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to take endto-end per-frame latency into the interactive regime ( 50 ms). We analyze the limiting factors of existing models by profiling the critical inference path of reference 1.3B-parameter model, common model size that balances speed and generation quality  (Fig. 2)  . We find that dominant costs lie not in diffusion denoising steps, but rather in operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates. For instance, single VAE decoding step takes as long as 3.5 DiT passes. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. First, we replace the VAE decoder with ConvNeXt-based (Liu et al., 2022) head that operates only in low spatial resolution, followed by single linear layer that unpatchifies and upsamples the latents to pixel dimensions, reducing decoding latency by 147 while matching quality. Furthermore, because the head is lightweight, training the model end-to-end in pixel-space (e.g., perceptual (Zhang et al., 2018) and GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014) losses) becomes practical, bypassing the reconstruction bottleneck of the VAE. Second, the baseline inference pipeline includes an additional DiT evaluation on each fully denoised latent solely to refine the KV cache (Sec. 3.3); we replace the DiT evaluation with lightweight network, reducing cache-update latency 10x without measurable degradation in quality. Finally, we perform multiple systemlevel, hardware-aware optimizations that specifically target the end-to-end per-frame critical path. Our techniques target components shared by many AR video diffusion models and are therefore complementary to advances in backbone architecture, such as hybrid transformers (Chen et al., 2026a), and improved distillation methods (Liu et al., 2026a). In the standard text-to-video (T2V) setting, where the model simply treats the current generated frame as input for generating the next, our quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that FastFrames establishes new Pareto frontier between generation quality and speed  (Fig. 1)  . The 1.3B variant achieves an end-to-end per-frame latency of 36 ms (28 RPS) on single B200 GPU at 832480 resolution (480p), matching the visual quality of state-of-the-art baseline (Zhao et al., 2026a) that is 7.6 slower. Scaling FastFrames to 14B improves visual fidelity while achieving 45 ms (22 RPS) on an 8 B200 GPU node. The T2V AR pipeline can be extended to accept controls between generation steps, such as camera poses (Jiang et al., 2026), 2D tracks (Shin et al., 2026), and 3D dynamics (Li et al., 2025b). We show that FastFrames enables fluid interactive experiences in two applications: camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation. 2 Figure 2 Inference pipeline and latency profiling for one autoregressive generation. State-of-the-art fewstep autoregressive video diffusion models generate each new frame by first updating the KV cache using the previous frames denoised latent (zi1 ) through DiT evaluation, then performing multiple denoising steps followed by VAE decoding. The color gradient of the model components denotes speed: from white (fastest operations) to red (slowest). (a) The fastest baseline, Causal Forcing++ (Zhao et al., 2026a), takes 271 ms to generate frame at 480p but only 30% of wall time is spent on diffusion sampling. (b) FastFrames reduces latency nearly 8 by replacing the nondenoising accessories with lightweight alternatives and performing systems-level optimizations to speed up each DiT evaluation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Accelerating diffusion sampling. Diffusion models require iterative sampling (Ho et al., 2020). Earlier work reduces the number of sampling steps using training-free accelerated samplers (Song et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022, 2025) or by training models to take larger steps along their sampling trajectories (Frans et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2025; Shaul et al., 2026). The state of the art relies on distribution matching (Yin et al., 2024b,a; Cui et al., 2026), where few-step student generator approximates the distribution of teacher network. Another line of work focuses on the inference cost of DiTs, including hybrid attention (Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a), sliding-window attention for long context (Xiao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), and layer pruning or model-size distillation (Fang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025b). smaller line of work focuses specifically on compressing or sparsifying the KV cache of autoregressive video diffusion models to reduce attention overhead (Ji et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2026). However, these methods are generally model-specific, so instead we target other components on the critical path. Our work builds on state-of-the-art few-step models, but we observe that the iterative denoising process is no longer the latency bottleneck. Reducing VAE decoding time. State-of-the-art video diffusion models perform diffusion in latent space (Blattmann et al., 2023), generally encoded via variational autoencoder (VAE) (Kingma & Welling, 2014). For instance, the Wan VAE (Wang et al., 2025) can perform up to 48 reduction in dimensionality. 3 This makes generation cheaper but pixel decoding becomes expensive. VAE decoders repeatedly upsample features in space and time, and apply dense 3D convolutions at each resolution. For example, tensor containing four 480832 frames requires convolution at approximately 1.6 million spatiotemporal positions. line of work aims to speed up VAEs (Boer Bohan, 2023; Buzovkin & Shilov, 2025) by reducing the number of parameters and removing expensive operations like attention and wide 3D convolutions. These methods gain up to 4 speedup but incur degradation in visual quality (Boer Bohan, 2025; Huang et al., 2025). Instead, we treat the pixel decoder as lightweight readout specific to frozen DiT, rather than general-purpose reconstruction problem. Our pixel head maintains visual quality while being two orders of magnitude faster. Systems-level optimizations. Systems-level techniques accelerate diffusion inference through more efficient scheduling and hardware utilization. Kodaira et al. (2025) and Bandyopadhyay et al. (2026) use batching and pipeline parallelism to improve streaming throughput but do not improve per-frame latency. StreamDiffusionV2 (Feng et al., 2026) emphasizes non-amortized time-to-first-frame but to the best of our understanding, this metric focuses on the start of stream, in contrast to our steady-state measurements. Optimized attention kernels (Dao, 2024), compilation and operator fusion (Ansel et al., 2024), and CUDA graph execution (Ghosh et al., 2025) reduce memory traffic and execution overhead. Weight and activation quantization (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Su et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b) reduce memory requirements and can accelerate computation with suitable hardware support. Distributed inference spreads computation across multiple GPUs through patch, sequence, and pipeline parallelism (Li et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025b, 2024). Our work incorporates many of these techniques.

sections.title: 3.1 Preliminaries: Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion Models
sections.content: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate video one latent chunk at time, using diffusion to synthesize each chunk conditioned on previously generated ones. We represent video sequence as z1:N = (z1, z2, . . . , zN ), where each chunk zi RCT HW contains 1 latent frames with channels and spatial resolution . Each latent frame corresponds to RGB frames, where is the temporal compression factor of the VAE. Generating larger chunks (e.g., one chunk = three latent frames, as in Self-Forcing (Huang et al., 2025)) is closer to bidirectional models and empirically easier to optimize, while generating smaller chunk (e.g., one chunk = one latent frame, as in Causal Forcing++ (CF++) (Zhao et al., 2026a) and FastFrames) is faster. The joint distribution factorizes autoregressively as p(z1:N ) = (cid:81)N i=1 p(zi z<i), where z<i = (z1, . . . , zi1) denotes the preceding chunks. Each conditional distribution is modeled by diffusion transformer (DiT), which generates the next chunk by iteratively denoising an initial noise sample and attends to the preceding chunks via KV cache. State-of-the-art models first convert pretrained bidirectional teacher model into an AR model, and then distill it into few-step AR student using distributionmatching distillation (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026). We refer readers to these works for training details. To examine the inference cost, we profile CF++, the fastest few-step AR video diffusion model at the time of writing. It is built on the Wan 2.1 1.3B-parameter backbone. Fig. 2 shows its inference latency on single B200 GPU, decomposed into three stages: KV-cache updates, diffusion sampling, and pixel rendering. We use its two-diffusion-step variant, which provides the best speed-quality tradeoff; reducing sampling steps to one significantly degrades visual quality while merely reducing latency by 15%. Each DiT evaluation takes 41.6 ms using BF16 precision, cuDNN attention backend (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026), and torch.compile (Ansel et al., 2024). The KV cache update is an additional DiT evaluation. Finally, the VAE decoder takes 147 ms to decode each generated latent into four RGB frames, resulting in total end-to-end latency of 271.8 ms. This profile suggests that our latency budget of 50 ms leaves room for only single diffusion sampling step. Instead, we replace the VAE with lightweight pixel rendering (Sec. 3.2) and accelerate KV cache updates (Sec. 3.3). Then, by reducing the latency of each DiT evaluation through systems-level optimizations (Sec. 3.4), we fit the full inference pipeline within the target latency. Our final 1.3B model runs in 36 ms on single B200 GPU, making it 7.6 faster than CF++. Our 14B model runs 10.6 faster than the fastest 4 Figure 3 Comparing pixel decoders. Our pixel decoder (right) renders thin structures and details like hair and raindrops while being two orders of magnitude faster than Wans VAE (left). single linear projection (middle) cannot render sharp outputs, but is sufficient for recognizing the scene and suggests that pixel rendering does not require an expensive decoder. open-source AR model of the same parameter count and achieves further 3.5 speedup when distributed across eight B200 GPUs.

sections.title: 3.2 Removing the VAE Decoder
sections.content: We first target the VAE decoder since it accounts for more than half of the end-to-end inference latency and alone exceeds our real-time budget 3. The VAE decoder only has 73M parameters (compared to the DiTs 1.3B) but repeatedly upsamples its features in space and time and applies dense 3D convolutions at each resolution. For example, tensor containing four 480832 frames requires convolution at approximately 1.6 million spatiotemporal positions. In light of recent advances in pixel diffusion models, we question whether such decoder is necessary when the DiT already produces rich and spatially contextualized features. For instance, JiT (Li & He, 2026) produces sharp images by mapping between image patches and transformer features using only linear projections. Thus, we first attempt replacing the VAE with single linear layer and train it with an MSE loss against the VAE decoded output, keeping the DiT frozen. We found that the outputs were blurry yet recognizable  (Fig. 3)  . We then increase the size of the pixel decoder, until arriving at our final architecture consisting of three causal 3D ConvNeXt-style blocks (Liu et al., 2022). Each block uses causal 333 depthwise convolution followed by channel-mixing MLP. All blocks operate only on the transformers low-resolution 213052 token grid. final linear layer converts each token into 41616 RGB patch, yielding an 84-frame, 480832 video. We discard the first three frames following the conventions of the Wan VAE, which does not temporally upsample the first frame. The total number of parameters is comparable (63.9M for ours vs. 73.3M), yet two orders of magnitude faster (1 ms vs. 147 ms). We train the pixel decoder using spatial and temporal reconstruction objectives. Let ˆypix denote the RGB video predicted by the ConvNeXt decoder, and let yVAE denote the output obtained by decoding the same final latent x0 with the frozen VAE. We optimize Lrec(ˆypix, yVAE) = λ1L1 + λMSELMSE + λgradLgrad + λtempLtemp + λmotionLmotion. (1) Here, λ1 = 0.5, λMSE = 5.0, λgrad = λtemp = 0.05, and λmotion = 0.5. All five terms are computed between ˆypix and yVAE. The L1 and LMSE terms enforce pixel-level fidelity, while Lgrad matches spatial image gradients 5 and Ltemp matches frame-to-frame changes. The motion-weighted term Lmotion emphasizes reconstruction errors in regions exhibiting motion in the VAE target. Complete definitions of the loss terms are provided in the supplement. In addition to reducing latency, our pixel decoder is less memory-intensive to optimize. For batch-sizeone, 81-frame video at 832480 resolution, VAE decoder update with BF16 precision and activation checkpointing requires approximately 68 GB of peak GPU memory, compared with approximately 5 GB for our pixel decoder. This makes it practical to optimize the decoder directly in pixel space with adversarial losses to improve sharpness and realism. We curated an internal dataset of 10K real videos and used frozen DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2026) ViTS/16 backbone as our discriminator. On each of layers 4, 8, and 12, we train two lightweight token-level discriminator heads: spatial classifier and temporal classifier that receives both the current patch feature and its change from the preceding frame. Let denote the six discriminator heads, let denote real video crop, and let ˆy denote generated crop. We use the following relativistic softplus discriminator objective (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2019): LD = 1 (cid:88) softplus(Dh(ˆy) Dh(y)) + λcenter [Dh(y) + Dh(ˆy)]2(cid:69) (cid:68) + λslope(R1 + R2), (2) hH where denotes averaging over clips, frames, and patch tokens, λcenter = 0.01, and λslope = 0.25. The terms R1 and R2 are finite-difference slope penalties on real and generated inputs, respectively (Lin et al., 2026). We estimate them on 25% of the clips by adding Gaussian RGB perturbations with standard deviation ϵ = 0.01. The generator consists of the frozen DiT and the trainable ConvNeXt pixel decoder. We continue using the reconstruction objective (Eq. 1) with the reverse relativistic comparison: Ladv = 1 (cid:88) hH softplus ( [Dh(ˆy) sg(Dh(y))]) , (3) where sg denotes stop-gradient. We cap the adversarial RGB-gradient magnitude relative to the reconstruction gradient for stable optimization. We also tried finetuning the DiT with low learning rate, but observed training instability. As seen in Fig. 3, our pixel decoder faithfully reconstructs thin structures like hair and raindrops. However, unlike the Wan VAE decoder, which can be shared across models of the same family (e.g., 1.3B and 14B variants), our pixel decoder must be finetuned for each individual model. Our main takeaway is that we can turn pixel decoding into lightweight readout rather than general-purpose reconstruction problem.

sections.title: 3.3 Faster KV Cache Updates
sections.content: Autoregressive video diffusion models attend to earlier frames through KV cache (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). Each DiT layer maintains its own cache, which holds an attention sink plus sliding window of recent entries. During each generation, the final denoising pass leaves the current chunks cache entries computed from noisy input. The baselines therefore run an additional DiT pass on the predicted clean latent ˆzi at = 0 and replace those entries with its keys and values (the KV cache write in Fig. 2). They discard the passs output prediction. In two-step diffusion setup, KV refinement accounts for one-third of DiT evaluations. We first investigate whether refinement is necessary. Naively removing the refinement leads to substantial degradation and training the model to use noisy cached features still produces noticeable artifacts (see supplement for visualizations). However, we hypothesize that lightweight network can replace the expensive DiT pass. We design KV refinement network with shared feature extractor and per-layer KV-repair heads. The feature extractor takes ˆzi and applies the DiTs frozen patch embedding followed by four lightweight transformer blocks trained from scratch. Each repair head takes these output features and its layers noisy keys and values to predict residual corrections. 6 Table 1 Quantitative comparisons in terms of end-to-end latency and VBench scores. All methods use the same evaluation prompts and seeds, run on one B200 GPU unless otherwise indicated, and are evaluated at approximately 480p using their officially supported dimensions. Green indicates latency that meets the interactive target ( 50 ms); yellow indicates sub-second latency (50 < latency < 1,000 ms). We measure steady-state latency with full cache. See the supplement for details. During training, we freeze the DiT and use the keys and values produced by the original DiT refinement pass to supervise residual corrections to the noisy cache. We train our network with two losses: direct KV reconstruction loss combining cosine distance and relative ℓ2 error, and an attention-output loss that compares the outputs obtained when subsequent chunks attend to the predicted versus target cache. The network performs comparably to the original refinement pass in terms of quantitative and qualitative comparisons, while taking approximately 2 ms for the 1.3B model and 6 ms for the 14B model on B200 GPU, around 20 and 12 faster respectively than the baselines refinement. We provide details in the supplement.

sections.title: 3.4 Systems-level Optimizations
sections.content: After reducing non-denoising overhead, DiT evaluations remain the main bottleneck to real-time generation. Free optimizations, including faster attention backends and torch.compile(), are already accounted for in the baseline profiling  (Fig. 2)  . First, we observe that the repeated structure of DiT evaluations offers opportunities to reuse computation. We maintain persistent KV-cache buffers and write new entries directly into their designated slots; precompute and store RoPE tables, text and timestep conditions; and fuse QKV projections into one larger matrix multiplication. Second, we find that per-frame AR generation can provide too few query tokens to fully utilize the GPU. We therefore split the KV sequence into segments processed in parallel, then combine their attention outputs using softmax merge. Concretely, for full KV cache of length 32,760, we found that splitting it into five segments of 6,552 each led to 13% latency reduction. Third, we reduce the overhead of launching and coordinating GPU work via CUDA graphs. Together, these optimizations bring the DiT evaluation latency from 41.6 ms to 16.4 ms for the 1.3B model on one B200 GPU at the full 32,760-token KV prefix and from 89.2 to 75.6 ms for the 14B model, corresponding to approximately 2.5 and 1.2 speedups. Next, we distribute computation across 8 B200 GPUs. We experimented with tensor parallelism, attentionhead parallelism, KV sharding, joint queryKV partitioning, and context parallelism (CP). Among them, 7 Figure 4 Qualitative comparisons. We compare FastFrames-S with Causal Forcing++ at 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with Krea-Realtime at 14B. Each example shows frames at 0 and 5 seconds. FastFrames-S achieves comparable visual sharpness to Causal Forcing++, such as the details in the sculpture (first example) and leaves (second example), while being nearly 8 faster. FastFrames-L achieves comparable visual realism to Krea-Realtime, including composition of paper origami dragon (third), and legible text of stay curious (fourth) while being 10 faster. See our website for video playback. only CP reduced computation sufficiently to justify communication overhead. CP partitions query tokens across GPUs and distributes both attention and feed-forward computation, requiring only one exchange of computed keys and values per transformer layer. We implement these exchanges using CUDA-graph8 compatible NVLink symmetric-memory gathers. This configuration reduces DiT latency from 16.4 to 5.8 ms for the 1.3B model and from 75.6 to 20.3 ms for the 14B model, corresponding to 2.8 and 3.7 speedups over their optimized single-GPU implementations.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Models and baselines. We build FastFrames on the Wan 2.1 backbone at two model sizes: FastFramesS with 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with 14B. We initialize FastFrames-S from the two-step Causal Forcing++ (CF++) checkpoint and finetune it using our method. We freeze the DiT and train our pixel decoder and KV refinement network against their respective targets. FastFrames-L required starting from the base bidirectional model. Following the training recipe in CF++, we converted Wan 2.1 14B into an autoregressive model, distilled it into few-step model, and trained it with DMD. Both FastFrames-S and FastFrames-L perform two-step diffusion sampling and generate one latent frame per autoregressive step. Quantitative comparisons. Tab. 1 provides quantitative comparison against bidirectional video generators and autoregressive models. The bidirectional models provide broader reference for generation quality and latency, while the autoregressive models provide direct comparisons. We report model size, latency, and VBench (Huang et al., 2024) scores. All models are evaluated using the same VBench prompts and seeds. We report end-to-end latency and compute RPS as its reciprocal in seconds, following the definitions in the introduction. For AR models, one response corresponds to an autoregressive generation unit; for bidirectional models, it corresponds to complete generated clip. Consequently, RPS does not credit method for producing multiple frames within one generation unit. We account for diffusion sampling, KV cache updates where applicable, and pixel rendering. For AR models, we measure latency at steady state after warm-up and with full KV cache. For bidirectional models, we let the model warm up and then generate the configured native clip lengths. All models are evaluated on B200 GPU unless otherwise specified, at approximately 480p using the models officially supported resolutions. We find that FastFrames matches corresponding baselines with the same Wan 2.1 backbone (Krea-Realtime vs. FastFrames-L, CF++ vs. FastFrames-S). Between FastFrames-S and CF++, which use the same DiT weights, we attribute the higher visual quality to end-to-end adversarial training in pixel space, which boosts realism and sharpness. None of the baselines meet the 50 ms latency target required for interactive applications. The fastest baseline, CF++, reaches 3.68 RPS at 272 ms, falling 5.4 short of the 20 RPS target. In contrast, FastFrames-S attains latency of 36 ms (27.8 RPS) on single B200 GPU and FastFrames-L attains 45 ms (22.2 RPS) on an 8-GPU node. FastFrames-S on 8 GPUs reaches 14 ms (71.4 RPS), while FastFrames-L on single GPU reaches 158 ms (6.33 RPS). Qualitative comparisons. Fig. 4 shows side-by-side comparison between FastFrames-S, FastFramesL, and their respective baselines. FastFrames-S maintains visual sharpness relative to CF++, capturing fine details like sculptures and leaves while being nearly 8 faster. FastFrames-L achieves realism, prompt adherence, composition, and text rendering capabilities comparable to Krea-Realtime while being over 10 faster. Fig. 4 also illustrates the improved capabilities of the 14B models relative to their 1.3B counterparts. The larger models produce more realistic lighting and shadows in the first two examples, better capture the folded-paper appearance of the origami dragon in the third, and render more legible text in the fourth. We encourage readers to view the supplementary videos on the project website. Interactive applications. We showcase FastFrames in interactive settings by accelerating cameraconditioned and physics-conditioned video generation: LingBot (Gao et al., 2026), family of cameraconditioned video models with 1.3B and 14B variants, and RealWonder (Liu et al., 2026c), 1.3B physicsconditioned video model. Our techniques transfer directly to these off-the-shelf models and yield large speedups, even over official code that already includes optimizations such as Ulysses sequence parallelism (Jacobs et al., 2024). Fig. 5 summarizes the latency profiles. On LingBot 1.3B, we reduce latency from 842 ms (the fastest official configuration, 2 GPUs) to 52 ms on 8 GPUs, 16 speedup. Times include diffusion sampling (four steps for LingBot and three for RealWonder), action conditioning, KV-cache updates, and pixel decoding. Our optimizations provide speedups of 3 to 22. See the project website for the video demonstration. both models approximately reach our target interactive latency. On LingBot 14B, latency drops from 1373 ms to 233 ms on 8 GPUs (5.9). These models remain slower than our T2V models because they require more diffusion sampling steps, predict multiple latent frames per autoregressive step, and need extra DiT computation to process additional conditioning. We show side-by-side comparison between the interactive demos on the project website; the original models exhibit noticeable lag while our optimized versions of LingBot 1.3B and RealWonder respond to user inputs fluidly.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented FastFrames, family of autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency by rethinking components of the inference pipeline often treated as fixed implementation details. Both our 1.3B and 14B variants achieve generation quality comparable to or better than their respective baselines. While our evaluation focuses on text-to-video generation at 480p on high-end GPUs, important directions for future work include adding action conditioning without increasing latency, scaling to higher resolutions, and supporting lighter hardware form factors. Improving long-term consistency and physical plausibility will further broaden the utility of video world models.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: We organize the appendix into the following sections: (A) Limitations and future work, (B) Additional latency profiling, (C) Architecture and training details of pixel decoder, (D) Architecture and training details of KV refinement network, and (E) Adaptation details of interactive applications. We encourage readers to view the videos on our website.

sections.title: A Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Resolution. Most baselines and base video models use 480p resolution, which we finetune from. Higher resolution like 720p or even 4K is desired for variety of applications like gaming and content creation. In the next section, we find that increasing resolution to 720p increases latency significantly; further optimization is required to bring high-res video generation into the interactive regime. Accessible hardware. We use B200 GPUs for our latency measurements in the main paper. While we assume compute will continue to become cheaper and more accessible, being able to run interactive video models on-device is an exciting possibility. Action conditions designed for lower latency. We applied FastFrames to off-the-shelf autoregressive models that were slower than their T2V counterparts. Training base models with lower latency in mind, such as concatenating camera poses in the channel dimension rather than the sequence dimension, without compromising quality, is essential for reducing latency.

However, we did not find detailed descriptions or breakdowns of those numbers and can only infer their profiling from source code. We found that Self-Forcing measured latency by generating video sequence of latent chunks (where each chunk 1 latent frame(s)), then dividing the total time by the number of chunks. However, earlier chunks are faster to generate due to an initially empty KV cache that gradually fills, so this average does not represent steady-state latency at long contexts. Occasionally, baselines provide ambiguous latency numbers without explanation; Causal Forcing++ (Zhao et al., 2026a) reports 270 ms for its 1, 2, and 4 step models without explanation. All of our profiling numbers include breakdown of the specific operation, and are measured at steadystate with full KV cache where applicable based on officially released configurations (e.g., KV=32760 for Self-Forcing and its follow-up works).

sections.title: C Architecture and Training Details of Pixel Decoder
sections.content: Our pixel decoder is causal ConvNeXt model operating directly on the pre-head features of the frozen two-step DiTs. For 21-frame latent sequence, the DiT produces 32,760 tokens on (21 30 52) spatiotemporal grid with channel width 1536. The head applies per-frame adaptive shift/scale modulation, (1 1) channel projection, and three ConvNeXt-style causal 3D residual blockstwo low-resolution blocks followed by one output blockusing depthwise (3 3 3) convolutions, channel-wise layer normalization, and width-4 pointwise GELU expansions. All convolutional processing remains at the DiT token resolution; the selected configuration has no learned temporal or spatial upsampler, latent adapter, displacement branch, auxiliary feature fusion, or post-RGB refiner. final per-token linear projection maps the 1536-dimensional features to (4 16 16 3) RGB values, which are unpatchified into 84 frames at (480 832) and aligned to the VAE convention by dropping the first three frames, yielding 81 output frames. The decoder contains 63.87M parameters and is causal in time, so each output block depends only on the current and preceding latent blocks. We train the pixel decoder using paired spatial-temporal reconstruction objective. Let ˆypix denote the RGB video predicted by the ConvNeXt decoder, and let yVAE denote the output obtained by decoding the same final latent x0 with the frozen VAE. Both videos are represented in the range [1, 1]. Our reconstruction objective is Lrec = 0.5 L1 + 5.0 LMSE + 0.05 Lgrad + 0.05 Ltemp + 0.50 Lmotion. The pixelwise terms are L1 = mean(ˆypix yVAE) and LMSE = mean((ˆypix yVAE)2). To preserve spatial structure, we match horizontal and vertical finite differences: (4) Lgrad = mean(h ˆypix hyVAE) + mean(w ˆypix wyVAE) . To preserve temporal dynamics, we match consecutive-frame differences: Ltemp = mean(t ˆypix tyVAE) . Finally, we place greater reconstruction weight on regions that move in the VAE target: (5) (6) Lmotion = meant>1,p[(1 + γ meanc tyVAE,t,c,p) meanc ˆypix,t,c,p yVAE,t,c,p] , γ = 10. (7) Here, h, w, and denote vertical, horizontal, and temporal finite-difference operators, respectively; indexes RGB channels; and indexes spatial locations. The multiplier γ controls how strongly moving target regions are emphasized within Lmotion, while the coefficient 0.50 controls the overall contribution of this term to Lrec. Using the vidprom_filtered_extended.txt file provided in Self-Forcings repo, we roll out the frozen DiT and VAE 150k times to get the input and output targets, running 4 optimization steps per rollout. We train on 32 B200 GPUs for about week; we find that validation loss and metrics (PSNR and SSIM) continue to improve steadily though slowly. 17 We take the last checkpoint and train with the adversarial setup as described in the main paper (Sec. 3.2). We train on 8 B200 GPUs and run 5000 rollouts per GPU and 4 optimization steps per rollout. Training completes in few hours.

sections.title: D Architecture and Training Details of KV Refinement Network
sections.content: As described in the main paper, we first investigate whether KV refinement is necessary, given that the last diffusion sampling step writes noisy KV cache for free. In Fig. 6, we find that removing KV refinement, even after training the model to learn to use the noisy KV cache, leads to drift and artifacts. These experiments motivate our design. Our KV refinement network is cache-repair module that replaces the expensive DiT evaluation of the baselines. Each DiT layer maintains its own KV cache, partitioned into one slice for each generated latent frame. During every diffusion evaluation for frame i, the KV tensors for that frame overwrite its current cache slice, while the slices for earlier frames remain available as causal context. At the final denoising step, the DiT still receives nonzero-noise latent, although it predicts the clean latent z0; consequently, the KV written to the current slice correspond to the noisy input. The baseline therefore performs an additional, non-denoising DiT forward pass on z0 with zero-noise time conditioning (t = 0), overwriting the same slice with clean-context KV. Instead, our network consumes the noisy K/V tensors from the final denoising pass together with the predicted z0, predicts corrected K/V tensors, and overwrites the same cache slice. Subsequent latent frames therefore attend to the repaired context without requiring the additional full DiT forward pass. shared stem maps the 1,560 patch tokens per frame from 1,536 to 768 channels, then applies four lightweight 8-head spatial self-attention blocks with 4 GELU MLPs and timestep-conditioned adaptive layer normalization. Each of the DiT layers has separate repair head that projects its noisy K/V, concatenates them with the shared pertoken z0 features, and predicts residual corrections. Keys are corrected in post-RoPE space and renormalized per attention head, while values receive learned residual and per-channel scale. All residual outputs are zero-initialized so the adapter initially behaves like the no-prime baseline. During inference, frame 0 retains real clean-prime anchor, while subsequent frames use the repaired K/V to overwrite their cache slots before the next frame is processed. The adapter is trained with the DiT and VAE frozen using teacher-forced targets from the real prime pass: the primary objective matches future attention outputs, supplemented by direct K/V reconstruction with approximately three times more weight on value than key errors, since we found that value corruption dominates the degradation.

sections.title: E Adaptation Details of Interactive Applications
sections.content: We use the official model and weights released by the authors. We follow the procedure described in Sec. 3 to train both the pixel decoder and the KV refinement network. Neither component requires large-scale training data. We simply roll out the models to create target pixels and clean keys and values on-the-fly. LingBot requires four diffusion sampling steps per autoregressive generation, and generates four latent frames at once. RealWonder requires three sampling steps and generates three latent frames at once. Both are substantially more expensive than our setup in FastFrames, which performs two sampling steps, and generates one latent frame at time. Thus, even the 1.3B models require 8 GPUs to reach interactive latency. RealWonder is slower than LingBot at the same parameter count due to its more expensive processing of its action conditions. Distilling these models to fewer steps and fewer latent frames per generation while maintaining output quality and adherence to conditions is important future work. 18 Figure 6 KV refinement ablation. Autoregressive baselines refine the KV cache using an additional DiT evaluation, which is costly but effective. Removing that refinement naively (third column) substantially degrades the scenes consistency; the objects in the scenes change over time. Even training without the refinement (fourth column) does not fix the problem. Either the subject changes over time (the face changes in the second example), or noticeable artifacts appear (clothing in the first example, fingers in the second example). Our KV refinement network (second column) replaces the DiT evaluation and performs equally while being an order of magnitude faster.
